newsitem.title: USA: U.S. government recommends polio vaccine change.
newsitem.headline: U.S. government recommends polio vaccine change.

text.p: Federal health officials on Wednesday recommended increased use of an injected polio vaccine because the oral vaccine that eradicated the disease can paralyse infants.

The Centres for Disease Control (CDC) accepted the recommendation of an advisory committee that said children should be given two shots of an inactivated vaccine, which is made from killed virus, followed by two doses of the oral vaccine.
Because the oral vaccine is made from weakened live virus, it causes eight to 10 cases of paralytic polio every year. The CDC said the new schedule would prevent most of those cases.

"This change will further ease parents' concern by routinely offering children the benefits of both polio vaccines," said CDC director Dr. David Satcher. "Parental awareness about vaccine options and the importance of vaccination is essential."
The recommendation said infants should be vaccinated at 2 months, 4 months, 12-18 months and 4-6 years of age.
In June, parents of young children with vaccine-associated polio urged a CDC advisory committee to shift to the inactivated vaccine, which is given as a shot.

The CDC said its recommendation "applied only to the United States" and other countries should continue to exclusively use the oral vaccine. Some experts have said eliminating the oral vaccine would send the wrong message to other countries and jeopardise efforts to eradicate polio worldwide by the year 2000.

The number of polio cases reported worldwide declined about 75 percent between 1988 and 1994. Almost 60 percent of remaining polio cases are in India. In 1954, before vaccine use became widespread, there were more than 18,000 cases of polio in the United States.
